content.title: About
content.content: Plantain is a large tropical fruit from the banana family that is typically eaten only after cooking. When prepared without added fat it retains a soft texture and a mildly sweet flavor, similar to a ripe banana but with a more pronounced starchy base.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Plantains are often called “cooking bananas” because raw they are too firm and starchy to eat.
Across cultures plantains are fried, boiled, baked, or steamed, each method giving a distinct taste.
In many African and Caribbean countries plantain is a staple carbohydrate, comparable to potatoes elsewhere.
There are several ripeness stages: green (unripe), yellow (partially ripe) and black (fully ripe), each with different sugar levels and texture.
Plantains are rich in resistant starch, which acts as a prebiotic supporting gut health.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Provides slowly digestible starch that offers sustained energy and helps maintain stable blood glucose.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis, supporting nervous system function.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in fluid balance and helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber and resistant starch promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Cooking without added fat keeps the dish low in calories from fat.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to banana family plants.

items.title: High glycemic index when fully ripe
items.content: Over‑ripe plantains can raise blood sugar quickly, which is important for people with diabetes.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Some varieties contain oxalates that may contribute to kidney stone formation if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Plantains can be boiled, baked, steamed, or mashed. They are commonly used in side dishes, soups, casseroles, and frittatas. Preparing them without oil preserves their natural flavor and keeps the meal lower in calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh plantains in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer, where they stay good for up to 5 days. Cooked pieces can be frozen in airtight containers for up to 3 months.
